Facebook Twitter Youtube Will i be able to see the Artemis II Moon mission orbiting the Moon ? Prev 1 2 3 Next Page 1 of 3 Recommended Posts I think this is the best place to put this one. It's Tuesday 31st and it looks like Wednesday 1/04/26 is the launch day (unless delayed again) for the Artemis II Moon orbital mission from NASA. Any experienced observers - imagers going to try and spot the Orbiter ? I have been thinking about this today as the news is building in hype to the launch and the first crewed return to the Moon for 50 years (orbital not a lander mission). I can see the ISS and various satellites. At 50x i can make out the basic H profile of the ISS from my garden. Now we factor in the Moon is very far away and the Artemis II is smaller than the ISS so i am guessing that if when i look at the Moon in several days time and see a small bright dot in Orbit.... a bit like seeing a tiny Starlink satellite in low earth orbit then i would have glimpsed the Orbiter. I doubt to see any more than a bright tiny dot. is anyone else going to have go at seeing/imaging and given that this is a new occurrence how do you rate your chances ? 1 Replies 52 Created Mar 31 Last Reply 2 dy Top Posters In This Topic 12 6 4 3 Posted Images I think I once read that the best Earth based telescope could only resolve features at the Moon’s distance down to 0.5 miles, but maybe a glint of light from the orbiter may get picked up ? 2 Author @dweller25 that's what i was expecting, a tiny bright dot catching/reflecting light. 1 It will be fun to have a look for it 😀 It's not doing a lap of the moon though as I understand, its like Apollo 13, on a free return path. Zoom around the back and then back. 1 Author Ahhh, can't say i have followed the mission plan, i assumed it was there for a survey mission so would get a few orbits in before returning. As far as I can surmise there is only two hopes. One is named Bob and the other is ? Well you can guess. The smallest thing I've seen in space was a tool bag that was let go by an astronaut working on the ISS back in 2008. This was visible with binoculars for a short while (24 hours or so) as a dim spot of light following the ISS across the sky. There was a similar loss back in 2023 but I don't think that one was visible from the UK. I'm not holding out any hopes of catching even a glimpse of Artemis II but I might observe the moon anyway, if it's clear 🙂 I can still clearly recall looking at the moon (no scope then - I was 9 years old) back in late July 1969 and thinking "wow !!! - there are people on there right now". And there were 😁 Edited March 31 by John I love the idea of sweeping the sky around the moon, hoping for a glimpse of a small bright dot. Might happen but maybe not when it's got to the moon. It would be visible in orbit, but I've no idea if it would stay visible for long. Unfortunately I'm visiting the MIL and haven't got any gear with me 😟 2 I imaged the JWST when it was about 750K miles from the earth but by then some layers of the tennis court sized sun shield had been deployed. It was just an insignificant light trail in a crowded star field. 13 I think I once read that the best Earth based telescope could only resolve features at the Moon’s distance down to 0.5 miles, but maybe a glint of light from the orbiter may get picked up ? Half a mile? Since November of last year that has been improved to 3 metres. Have a look at my recent post about this. Half a mile? Since November of last year that has been improved to 3 metres. Have a look at my recent post about this. Expand Clever but not a lot of help to a budding Patrick Moore and his ST-80 ... 😉 Author Might be beyond an ST-80 i suspect an image or two from others around the world may catch a bright dot in the Moon's orbit with better equipment. I shall be looking depending on clouds 😁 From Google: Key Details on Ground-Based Imaging The Virtual Telescope Project: Gianluca Masi, an astronomer with the Virtual Telescope Project, captured imagery of the Orion capsule while it was in deep space on its way to the Moon. Difficulty: While it was possible to track, Orion was quite faint because it was hundreds of thousands of miles from Earth. Tracking Data: Amateur astronomers used tracking data, such as NASA's Artemis Real-time Orbit Website (AROW), to pinpoint the location of the spacecraft for imaging. ----- From the above, it appears unlikely that amateurs will be able to image Artemis II at the distance of the Moon. A tool bag at 400 miles altitude will subtend a much greater angle at the Earth's surface than the Artemis capsule at lunar distance. Edited March 31 by Mandy Daniels Removed double negative 3 I still like the idea of looking. 4 is anyone else going to have go at seeing/imaging and given that this is a new occurrence how do you rate your chances ? I would say nil 4 I tried with some of the later Apollo missions when I was a small boy with a small reflector. Total failure. However, it was fantastic attempting to see the lunar lander on the surface… I mean just looking at the right spot knowing that there were people there - fantastic times! 4 Maybe get lucky with a solar panel reflection? 1 Out of interest. My late father had a job in the States in the 1960’s. As a treat I was taken to the Kennedy Space Centre. Even though I was 5 yrs old I can well remember seeing Apollo 10 (must have been rollout) off in the distance. Something I’ll never forget! PS - I was JUST 6 yrs old! Edited April 1 by PeterStudz 9 Out of interest. My late father had a job in the States in the 1960’s. As a treat I was taken to the Kennedy Space Centre. Even though I was 5 yrs old I can well remember seeing Apollo 10 (must have been rollout) off in the distance. Something I’ll never forget! PS - I was JUST 6 yrs old! Oi ! You said you were only five! Are you sure it wasn’t a poster on yer bedroom wall?! 1 Then there is that every second of its orbit around the moon will be calibrated to the inth! Some one will claim..” I’ve got it! I’ve got it! There it is..see it? Just there”..( hot pixel ) who’s going to tell him? 1 On 01/04/2026 at 18:13, Chaz2b said: Oi ! You said you were only five! Are you sure it wasn’t a poster on yer bedroom wall?! I’m at that age where I have trouble remembering how old I am…. 21 again 😀 1 On 31/03/2026 at 20:52, John said: The smallest thing I've seen in space was a tool bag that was let go by an astronaut working on the ISS back in 2008. This was visible with binoculars for a short while (24 hours or so) as a dim spot of light following the ISS across the sky. There was a similar loss back in 2023 but I don't think that one was visible from the UK. I'm not holding out any hopes of catching even a glimpse of Artemis II but I might observe the moon anyway, if it's clear 🙂 I can still clearly recall looking at the moon (no scope then - I was 9 years old) back in late July 1969 and thinking "wow !!! - there are people on there right now". And there were 😁 Expand My memory might be playing tricks but I recall I was able, through 15x56 binoculars, to see that 2023 tool bag, it wasn't difficult. I also recall it was slightly ahead of the ISS as it went over. 1 If Artemis is orbiting the Moon, and it’s now approaching a full Moon (when viewed from Earth) then surely the far-side of the Moon will be in darkness? Wouldn't the best time to orbit the far-side of the Moon be when it’s a New Moon on Earth and the far-side is facing the Sun? I have to say that I’m in the dark over this😉 On 02/04/2026 at 08:05, Joken said: If Artemis is orbiting the Moon, and it’s now approaching a full Moon (when viewed from Earth) then surely the far-side of the Moon will be in darkness? Wouldn't the best time to orbit the far-side of the Moon be when it’s a New Moon on Earth and the far-side is facing the Sun? I have to say that I’m in the dark over this😉 In six days time, when Artemis II arrives at the Moon, it will be approaching last quarter, so roughly half of the far side will be in sunlight. They have to launch when they have to launch as there are limited launch windows that are only open for a short time. You grab the first one you can and go for it. If the launch has to be postponed for technical reasons you try again in the next launch window and so on. I hope this helps.
